pulls.title: Use an explicit response_model as the item type on streaming endpoints
pulls.body:
Discussed in https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/16382.

On a streaming (generator) endpoint, `response_model` is only turned into a per-item field when it is left to the return annotation. Passing it explicitly silently disables both validation and the `response_model_*` options, and leaves the OpenAPI `itemSchema` empty:

```python
class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    secret: str

@app.get("/stream", response_model=Item, response_model_exclude={"secret"})
def stream():
    yield Item(name="public", secret="private")
```

Before this change the endpoint streams `{"name": "public", "secret": "private"}`, so a field the developer asked to exclude is served to the client, and the OpenAPI response is `{"application/jsonl": {"itemSchema": {}}}`. Writing `response_model=Iterable[Item]` instead does not help: it is rejected outright as an invalid response field.

`_populate_api_route_state` resolves the stream item type only inside the `isinstance(response_model, DefaultPlaceholder)` branch. With an explicit model, `route.stream_item_type` stays `None`, `stream_item_field` is never built, and `_serialize_data` falls back to `jsonable_encoder` plus `json.dumps`, which is the path that skips validation and the exclusion options.

An explicit `response_model` on a streaming endpoint now feeds `stream_item_field` the same way the return annotation does, and both the item type and an iterable of it are accepted. Afterwards the endpoint above streams `{"name": "public"}` and its OpenAPI response carries `itemSchema: {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Item"}`.

The new branch only applies to generator endpoints whose response class is the default placeholder (JSONL) or `EventSourceResponse` (SSE), and it keeps the existing `ServerSentEvent` exclusion, since that is a transport wrapper rather than a data model. Non-streaming endpoints, bare iterables and return-annotation streams are untouched.

## Tests

`tests/test_stream_explicit_response_model.py` covers sync and async generators, `Iterable[Item]` and `AsyncIterable[Item]`, `response_model_exclude` and `response_model_exclude_none`, SSE, per-item validation, and the OpenAPI schema, together with a non-streaming endpoint to pin that its behaviour is unchanged. On `master` the module fails at import, because `response_model=Iterable[Item]` raises `FastAPIError`.

The rest of the suite passes: 2046 passed, 12 skipped (`tests/`, excluding `benchmarks` and `test_tutorial`, which need optional extras not installed here).

pulls.title: 🐛 Prevent stale endpoint context cache entries
pulls.body:
## Problem

`_extract_endpoint_context()` caches endpoint metadata by `id(func)` without retaining or validating the function object. After an endpoint is collected, Python can reuse that id for another endpoint, causing validation errors and logs to report the wrong file, line, or function.

## Solution

Store a weak reference alongside each cached context and validate the referenced object with `is` before using a cache hit. Callable objects that do not support weak references are still handled correctly and are recomputed instead of being retained.

## Testing

- `uv run pytest -q tests/test_endpoint_context_cache.py tests/test_custom_route_class.py tests/test_custom_middleware_exception.py tests/test_callable_endpoint.py` (10 passed)
- `uv run mypy fastapi/routing.py` (passed)
- `uv run ty check fastapi/routing.py` (passed)
- `uv run bash scripts/test.sh` (3,347 passed, 18 skipped, 5 xfailed locally; the optional CLI test was unavailable because `fastapi[standard]` was not installed)
- Fork preflight run [35815878739](https://github.com/rksharma-owg/fastapi/actions/runs/35815878739) passed the full test script on Ubuntu 3.13, macOS 3.10, and Windows 3.12 for commit `914469e4cefd8085abd3020c470a8c2e022bdd16`.

Fixes #16390

pulls.title: 👷 Fix coverage badge: keep Smokeshow HTML under size limit and fail on upload errors
pulls.body:
The coverage badge in the README currently shows `coverage ??%`. The badge worker reports:

```
No status found which matched regex ^coverage, status descriptions: []
```

No `smokeshow / coverage` status has been posted on `master` since #14992 (2026-02-27). The last commits before it (e.g. 4fce9ce, 728b097) have `Coverage 100.00%`; every code commit after it has none.

## Root cause

#14992 replaced coverage's `dynamic_context = "test_function"` with pytest-cov's `--cov-context=test`. pytest-cov records one context per parametrized case **and** per phase (`|setup`, `|run`, `|teardown`), e.g.:

```
Linux-py3.13-no-deprecation|tests/test_request_params/test_cookie/test_optional_str.py::test_optional_alias_by_alias[/optional-alias]|run
```

The combined data now has ~20k contexts, and with `show_contexts = true` the generated `htmlcov` grew to **~68 MB**, over Smokeshow's 50 MB site limit. Every upload fails with:

```
ERROR! ... status=429 response=429: You've exceeded the site size limit of 52428800.
```

Since the status is only posted after a successful upload, it's never set.

This went unnoticed because the retry loop in `smokeshow.yml` ends with `sleep 1` when all 5 attempts fail, so the step exits 0 and the Smokeshow workflow is green.

## Changes

* `test.yml`: generate the HTML report with `--omit "tests/*"`. This keeps the per-test contexts for `fastapi/` and `docs_src/` (the useful part, "which test covers this line"), while dropping the per-file pages for the test files themselves. `coverage report --fail-under=100` is unchanged and still checks tests.
* `smokeshow.yml`: exit with an error if all upload attempts fail, so this kind of breakage is visible.

## Verification

Using the coverage artifacts from the latest `master` Test run (50113da):

| | HTML size | total |
|---|---|---|
| current | 68 MB | 100% |
| with `--omit "tests/*"` | 35 MB | 100% |

(For reference, disabling `show_contexts` entirely gives 41 MB; this approach keeps contexts and leaves more headroom.)

Also checked the upload loop with a stubbed command: exits `1` when every attempt fails, `0` on success.

pulls.title: 🐛 Fix endpoint context shared and mutated across requests
pulls.body:
_extract_endpoint_context() caches the context dict per endpoint function and returned the cached dict itself. The request handler (and the WebSocket handler) then set endpoint_ctx["path"] on it, mutating the shared cached object.

When the same endpoint function is used by more than one route (or the same route handles concurrent requests), the path stored in a RequestValidationError / ResponseValidationError could be overwritten by another request, so error messages and logs reported the wrong route.

Return a copy of the cached context so each request gets its own dict.

pulls.title: fix: serialize WebSocket validation errors to JSON string in close reason
pulls.body:
The default `websocket_request_validation_exception_handler` currently passes the result of `jsonable_encoder(exc.errors())` directly to `WebSocket.close()` as the `reason`.

`jsonable_encoder(exc.errors())` returns a list, while `WebSocket.close()` expects `reason` to be a `str | None`. As a result, WebSocket request-validation errors can cause the exception handler itself to fail instead of closing the connection with the intended `1008` policy-violation code.

This change serializes the validation errors with `json.dumps()` before passing them to `WebSocket.close()`. The reason is therefore a valid string containing machine-readable JSON.

A regression test was added to verify that:

- WebSocket request-validation failures close with code `1008`.
- The close reason is a string.
- The reason contains the expected validation error.
- The behavior fails with the previous implementation and passes with this fix.

The change is intentionally minimal and does not alter the validation behavior or the WebSocket close code.

issues.title: RFC Always store fitted attributes as Numpy
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

This is an issue related to #34152 but is also a standalone issue.

While thinking about #34152 and working on #34324 I thought that it might be a good idea if the fitted attributes of an estimator were always Numpy arrays. The current plan is to store fitted attributes in the namespace/device of `X`.

Reasons to do this:
1. users most often use fitted attributes for inspection/debugging/plotting. Having them in a consistent array namespace makes this easy to do. If the namespace is input dependent then you have to change your debugging/plotting code. Say you run the same script on a machine with a CUDA GPU and on your laptop with no GPU. While it is not difficult to use write code that uses `move_to()` to conditionally bring the attributes to Numpy for plotting, it is tedious.
2. Today attributes are Numpy, by keeping them Numpy we remove one source of bugs/differences. Enabling array API by default would not change this
3. Part of #34324 that is not great/tricky is dealing with estimators that sometimes support array API. For example for some hyper-parameter values array API is supported and for some not. The tricky question: What should the type of the fitted attributes be?
4. You can `fit` with one array namespace/device and `predict` with a different one without any conversion
5. An estimator fitted with pytorch/CUDA can be unpickled on a machine without CUDA and even without pytorch

Something to check is how much overhead/performance loss we get in `predict` and other inference methods if we have to convert the fitted attributes relevant for predicting from Numpy to the array namespace of the input each time. Though I suspect that conversion is fast. It might add appreciable overhead if you are predicting on very few samples, but the absolute time will be short in those cases (and you could just use the CPU?). We would need to introduce a way to make it easy to convert fitted attributes to Numpy in each estimator to avoid lots of boilerplate. What are other reasons to not do this?

What do others think?

issues.title: Lasso(alpha) = SGDRegressor(alpha, penalty="l1"), but Ridge(alpha) = SGDRegressor(alpha / len(train_set))

labels.name: Needs Decision
labels.description: Requires decision

labels.name: Breaking Change
labels.description: Issue resolution would not be easily handled by the usual deprecation cycle.

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

`Ridge` and `SGDRegressor` are inconsistent in the way they handle the regularization hyperparameter `alpha`:

* `Ridge(alpha=alpha)` is equivalent to `SGDRegressor(alpha / m, penalty="l2", ...)`, where `m` is the training set size.
* But `Lasso(alpha=alpha)` is equivalent to `SGDRegressor(alpha, penalty="l1", ...)`, which is great.

Looking at the source code of `SGDRegressor`, it looks like `l1` and `l2` are consistent, so it must be a problem with `Ridge`. Perhaps it should be modified to divide `alpha` by `m`?

Is it just historical, or is there a rationale behind this?


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, Ridge, SGDRegressor

alpha = 0.1
m = 100

np.random.seed(42)
X = 2 * np.random.rand(m, 1)
y = 4 + 3 * X + np.random.randn(m, 1)

ridge = Ridge(alpha=alpha)
ridge.fit(X, y)
print("Ridge:", ridge.intercept_, ridge.coef_)

sgd_reg = SGDRegressor(
                       loss="squared_error", penalty="l2", alpha=alpha / m,
                       max_iter=10_000, tol=None, eta0=0.0001,
                       learning_rate="constant", random_state=42)
sgd_reg.fit(X, y.ravel())
print("SGDRegressor with l2:", sgd_reg.intercept_, sgd_reg.coef_)

lasso = Lasso(alpha=alpha)
lasso.fit(X, y)
print("Lasso:", lasso.intercept_, lasso.coef_)

sgd_reg = SGDRegressor(loss="squared_error", penalty="l1", alpha=alpha,
                       max_iter=10_000, tol=None, eta0=0.0001,
                       learning_rate="constant", random_state=42)
sgd_reg.fit(X, y.ravel())
print("SGDRegressor with l1:", sgd_reg.intercept_, sgd_reg.coef_)
```


### Expected Results

I would expect the `Ridge` model to be different from the `SGDRegressor` model, since it does not use the same `alpha` value. Instead, they are equal.

### Actual Results

But here is the output of the previous code:

```
Ridge: [4.22250784] [[2.76223165]]
SGDRegressor with l2: [4.22261191] [2.76235098]
Lasso: [4.48341837] [2.48477396]
SGDRegressor with l1: [4.4834874] [2.48492104]
```

As you can see, the `Ridge` model is equivalent to `SGDRegressor(alpha=alpha / m, ...)` instead of `SGDRegressor(alpha=alpha, ...)`. But `Lasso(alpha)` is equivalent to `SGDRegressor(alpha=alpha, penalty="l1", ...)`.

### Versions

Running on Colab:

```
System:
    python: 3.7.12 (default, Sep 10 2021, 00:21:48)  [GCC 7.5.0]
executable: /usr/bin/python3
   machine: Linux-5.4.104+-x86_64-with-Ubuntu-18.04-bionic

Python dependencies:
          pip: 21.1.3
   setuptools: 57.4.0
      sklearn: 1.0.1
        numpy: 1.19.5
        scipy: 1.4.1
       Cython: 0.29.24
       pandas: 1.1.5
   matplotlib: 3.2.2
       joblib: 1.1.0
threadpoolctl: 3.0.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

issues.title: FeatureAgglomeration.inverse_transform fails on list/DataFrame input, including its own set_output result

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I work in AI, ML, DS and use scikit-learn for preprocessing and modeling pipelines, usually with set_output(transform="pandas").

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`FeatureAgglomeration.inverse_transform` indexes its input directly (`X[..., inverse]`) without validating it, so anything that isn't a numpy array fails, including the pandas/polars output that `set_output` makes the estimator itself return.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import FeatureAgglomeration

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(10, 4)
fa = FeatureAgglomeration(n_clusters=2).fit(X)

fa.inverse_transform([[1.0, 2.0]])      # TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple

fa.set_output(transform="pandas")
fa.inverse_transform(fa.transform(X))   # pandas InvalidIndexError
```

### Expected Results

Same result as passing the equivalent ndarray (the docstring says X is array-like of shape (n_samples, n_clusters) or (n_clusters,)).

### Actual Results

- list: `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple`
- pandas (including the estimator's own `set_output(transform="pandas")` output): `InvalidIndexError` / `KeyError`
- polars: `DuplicateError`

A plain ndarray works.

### Versions

```shell
scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.0.6, polars 1.44.2, numpy 2.5.3 (main has the same code).
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes. I have a fix (validate with `check_array(X, ensure_2d=False)` in `inverse_transform`, plus tests for list/pandas/polars/1-D input) and would like to open the PR once this is triaged.

Found with AI assistance (Claude); I verified the repro.

issues.title: Add Accumulated local effects (ALE) to inspection

labels.name: Moderate
labels.description: Anything that requires some knowledge of conventions and best practices

issues.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'd love to push the inspection module further by adding Accumulated local effects (ALE) from Apley 2020. A great description can be found in Christoph's online book https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/ale.html

ALE fix the problem of partial dependence that they force the model to be evaluated on impossible or rare feature combinations. ALE are defined for numeric features that can be binned. From both bin edges, the slope of the partial dependence is calculated locally, i.e., only using observations in the bin. The slopes from all bins are cumsummed and vertically centered to the average response or prediction.

### Reference

Apley, Daniel W., and Jingyu Zhu. 2020. Visualizing the Effects of Predictor Variables in Black Box Supervised Learning Models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology, 82 (4): 1059–1086. doi:10.1111/rssb.12377.

### Describe your proposed solution

Pseudo code to calculate ALE for one feature:

``` py
pd_slopes = np.zeros_like(bins)

for i, bin in enumerate(bins):
  X_bin = pick n_per_bin = 200 rows from data in bin
  if X_bin is empty:
    next
  pd = partial_dependence_brute(model, X_bin, grid = [lower bin edge, upper bin edge], sample_weights)
  pd_slopes[i] = pd[1] - pd[0]

return np.cumsum(pd_slopes)
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

issues.title: Prevent CPU over-subscription when using thread pools, similar to what process pools do

labels.name: free-threading
labels.description: PRs and issues related to support for free-threaded CPython (a.k.a. nogil or no-GIL, PEP 703)

labels.name: Parallelism and scalability
labels.description: All things related to efficient handling of cores via thread-based or process-based parallelism.

issues.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Process pools in sklearn will limit the number of threads used by OpenMP and BLAS. Thread pools will not set any limits.

Consider the following program, which lists how many threads are set for OpenMP/OpenBLAS/etc:

```python
import joblib, sys
from sklearn.utils.parallel import Parallel, delayed
import threadpoolctl

def print_thread_pool_sizes():
    for info in threadpoolctl.threadpool_info():
        print(info["user_api"], info["internal_api"], f"threads: {info['num_threads']}")

with joblib.parallel_config(backend=sys.argv[1]):
    Parallel(n_jobs=-1)([delayed(print_thread_pool_sizes)()])
```

When run under the default backend, the loky process pool, I get:

```
$ python nested-parallelism.py loky
blas openblas threads: 1
blas openblas threads: 1
openmp openmp threads: 1
```

When run under the threading joblib backend, I get:

```
$ python nested-parallelism.py threading
blas openblas threads: 20
blas openblas threads: 20
openmp openmp threads: 20
```

This can lead to significant CPU oversubscription, depending on the semantics of the library:

* When using OpenBLAS, you will get a total of 40 (20 + 20) threads, since the limit is for a single thread pool shared by the whole process.
* When using OpenMP, you will get 400 (20 * 20) threads, since the limit is _per operation starting a thread pool._

The result is code that runs slower, wasting CPU cycles, and not actually achieving any more work.

### Describe your proposed solution

There are a number of scenarios:

**Scenario 1: All cores:** If the number of threads in a thread pool is the same as the number of (available) CPU cores, setting the OpenMP/BLAS limit to 1 will work correctly: no oversubscription, no cores sitting idle.
 
**Scenario 2: All cores but 1 or 2:** If the requested number of threads/processes is negative number `-N` in joblib, this is defined as "number of available cores + 1- N". I.e. this semantically suggests the users wants to saturate the cores, but leave a few cores for other tasks. Typically N will be small, e.g. 2 to leave one core free but use all others. In this case again setting the OpenMP/BLAS limit to 1 is the right thing to do.

**Scenario 3: A hard-coded small number of cores, less than available cores:** The remaining case is most likely when the number of cores is limited due to the way the algorithm works. For process pools joblib will already automatically set the number of threads in OpenMP/BLAS to `max(cpu_count() // effective_n_jobs, 1)`. So for example if you have 10 cores and only starting a pool of size 5, OpenMP/BLAS will each be set to allow 2 threads. In a process pool, this works fine.

For a top-level thread pool, this heuristic works fine for OpenMP but _not_ OpenBLAS, since the meaning of "2" is different: for OpenMP it means "2 threads for every operation started in the 5 threads, for a total of 2 * 5 == 10 threads", for OpenBLAS it means "2 threads for the whole process, for a total of 5 + 2 threads."

So this suggests two options; one could choose one, the other, or both:

1. Documentation for algorithms with limited parallelism, suggesting that it's better to use processes in order to utilize all cores.
2. Custom settings per parallelism mechanism: set OpenMP to `max(cpu_count() // effective_n_jobs, 1)` and BLAS to `cpu_count()`. This could still lead to oversaturation in certain edge cases, but perhaps it's not as bad. 

> As a follow-up it looks like MKL at least can due OpenMP-style configuration, with a different API than the one `threadpoolctl` uses.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

This could be implemented in joblib, rather than in sklearn, but that's a more generic context; there are additional threaded libraries that it might grow support for over time, whereas sklearn has more restricted set. Still, this arguably also be done as the default joblib policy for thread pools.

### Additional context

`joblib.cpu_count()` is aware of CPU resource constraints when running inside Linux containers, so its notion of "all available cores" is usually quite accurate.

I am happy to implement this.

I have also tested this [on actual code](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/compose/plot_compare_reduction.html), and `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` on an all-cores thread pool makes the resulting calculation run faster and reduce involuntary context switches. This is not a perfect experiment since OpenBLAS in threaded mode is often _slower_ than single-threaded OpenBLAS for small tasks, so a better experiment would be with some code that uses OpenMP, if someone can suggest one.

issues.title: `from sklearn.model_selection import *` raises ImportError since 1.8.0
issues.body:
### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm a CS student and regular scikit-learn user, mostly through model_selection. I ran into this while star-importing the module in a notebook and traced it back to a specific commit. First time filing a bug here.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`from sklearn.model_selection import *` raises an ImportError on 1.8.0+. It worked in 1.7.2, and every other public submodule still star-imports fine.

The cause: `HalvingGridSearchCV` and `HalvingRandomSearchCV` are listed in `__all__` (in `sklearn/model_selection/__init__.py`), but the module's `__getattr__` deliberately raises ImportError for both until you import `enable_halving_search_cv`. Star-import pulls every name in `__all__`, so it hits that guard and fails. The two names were added to `__all__` in #31847 (the ruff absolute-imports cleanup); before that they weren't exported.

Impact: any notebook or script doing `from sklearn.model_selection import *` breaks on upgrade to 1.8.0, with an error that looks unrelated to what the user actually did.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import *
```

### Expected Results

Star-import succeeds like it did in 1.7.2, without exporting the experimental Halving classes.

### Actual Results

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File ".../sklearn/model_selection/__init__.py", line 100, in __getattr__
    raise ImportError(
ImportError: HalvingGridSearchCV is experimental and the API might change without any deprecation cycle. To use it, you need to explicitly import enable_halving_search_cv:
from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.10 (tags/v3.12.10:0cc8128, Apr  8 2025, 12:21:36) [MSC v.1943 64 bit (AMD64)]
   machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0

Also reproduces on 1.8.0.
```

issues.title: Declare metadata properties to be used by the routers

labels.name: Needs Decision
labels.description: Requires decision

labels.name: Metadata Routing
labels.description: all issues related to metadata routing, slep006, sample props

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

When working on https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34263, I realized that `Pipeline` may not be the only place where we need to specify metadata that needs to be transformed like `X`.

There are several estimators that transform `X` internally (e.g. KMeans centers `X`). Now that they're going to become routers, they'll need to be able to transform some metadata, like `X_val`. I would like to avoid introducing `transform_input` in all these estimators.

On a related topic, meta-estimators with a CV split the metadata like `X` when it has the same length. This is very brittle and a well known issue. For instance if you pass a `X_val` that has the same size a `X` to a grid search, it will be split, and thus the callback won't receive the full `X_val`.

What's currently missing from metadata-routing to gracefully handle these 2 uses cases is a way to declare some properties for the metadata that you request. Discussing with @FrancoisPgm we've thought about a few alternatives:

- Add the possibility to declare additional property at request time. Something like:
  ```py
  LogisticRegression().set_fit_request(sample_weight=(True, MetadataProperties(split_like_X=True)))
  # or
  HistGradientBoostingClassifier().set_fit_request(X_val=(True, MetadataProperties(transform_like_X=True)))
  ```

  It adds more verbosity and burden on the user.

- Declare it only once using a kind of global registry, e.g.
  ```py
  sklearn.metadata_properties(sample_weight=MetadataProperties(split_like_X=True))
  ```

  Still adds some verbosity, except that it can be done once and not in all requests. The burden is still on the user side.

- Declare the property at the estimator level, maybe as a tag, maybe something else:
  ```py
  class LogisticRegression:

      metadata_properties = {
          "sample_weight": MetadataProperties(split_like_X=True)
      }

      def fit(X, y, sample_weight):
          ...
  ```

  The burden is on the developer side. The property is defined by the consumer that knows what it expects. No extra verbosity on the user side.

where MetadataProperties is a small dataclass like
```py
  @dataclass
  class MetadataProperties
      split_like_X: bool = False
      transform_like_X: bool = False
```


Writing this I realized that the 3rd option really feels more appropriate. I'm leaving the first 2 options for comparison. Ping @adrinjalali @StefanieSenger @ogrisel @FrancoisPgm what do you think ?

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Found while reviewing #34957.

`BaggingClassifier`/`BaggingRegressor` with `max_features < 1.0` (or `bootstrap_features=True`) fit each sub-estimator on `X[:, features]`, but they forward routed metadata as-is. So when `X_val` is routed to `HistGradientBoosting*`, the sub-estimator gets a full-width `X_val` while it was fitted on a subset of columns, and it raises:

```
ValueError: X has 20 features, but HistGradientBoostingClassifier is expecting 10 features as input.
```

The root cause is more general than Bagging: routers treat metadata as opaque, and only know how to slice "sample-aligned" metadata on rows (`_check_method_params`). They have no notion of "feature-aligned" metadata like `X_val`, which should get the same column selection as `X`. This seems closely related to #34270 (declaring metadata properties to be used by the routers).

issues.title: Investigation: conda-forge scikit-learn slower than PyPI (ExtraTrees case)
issues.body:
While looking at [builds comparison results](https://probabl-ai.github.io/scikit-learn-benchmarks/builds_comparison.html) from my benchmarks (https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks), I noticed `ExtraTrees*.fit` was often ~25% slower on conda-forge builds of
scikit-learn 1.9.0 than on PyPI wheels.

Two distinct bugs were found along the way; only the second one explains the slowdown:

1. **O3 vs O2** (documented in #34865): `-O3` in meson doesn't survive an environment `CFLAGS` that also sets `-O2` (which conda-forge's compiler activation does).

2. **Version of `glibc`** (cause of the slowdown): conda-forge compiles scikit-learn against a `sysroot_linux-64=2.17` (glibc 2.17, from 2012-12-25). That old glibc's `<math.h>` defines the `isnan()` macro as a dispatch to glibc-internal `__isnanf`/`__isnan` functions instead of `__builtin_isnan*`. GCC can't recognize or inline those, so `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx`'s `isnan(value)` calls — sitting in the hottest loop of tree-building (`find_min_max`, `partition_samples`) — become genuine non-inlined function calls. This is `fit`-specific (confirmed: `predict`, which doesn't call these functions, shows no slowdown) and fully reproduced from source once the exact sysroot was pinned.


This is very likely **not scikit-learn-specific**: any conda-forge package with a hot-loop `isnan()`/`isinf()` call is plausibly exposed the same way.

~~=> TODO: Open an issue in conda-forge~~ Done: I posted a comment here: https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compiler-activation-feedstock/issues/108

### Proposed fix

Replace `from libc.math cimport isnan` / `isnan(value)` in `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` (and any other tree/HGB hot loop doing the same) with the self-inequality NaN test `value != value`. Pure comparison, nothing to inline, immune to this class of bug on any compiler/libc, forever.

### Root cause, in detail

*(pure LLM write-up)*

<details>

`sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` (`DensePartitioner.find_min_max`, `.partition_samples`) and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` call `isnan(value)` on `float32_t` data, via `from libc.math cimport isnan`. This runs once per sample per feature scan during `fit`; never during `predict`.

The feedstock's CI pin file (`.ci_support/linux_64_python3.12.____cpython.yaml` at the 1.9.0 release commit) sets `c_stdlib: sysroot`, `c_stdlib_version: '2.17'`. That sysroot's `math.h` has:

```c
#  define isnan(x) \
     (sizeof (x) == sizeof (float) ? __isnanf (x) \
      : sizeof (x) == sizeof (double) ? __isnan (x) : __isnanl (x))
```

Once the preprocessor expands this, the identifier `isnan` is gone from
the translation unit — GCC has nothing left to recognize as a builtin, so
`__isnanf` (an ordinary external glibc symbol, not a compiler intrinsic)
gets a real out-of-line call. Modern glibc instead defines `isnan(x)` as
`__builtin_isnan(x)` directly, which GCC folds to 2 instructions
(`ucomiss`/`setp`). PyPI/manylinux wheels don't hit this because they're
built with devtoolset-style toolchains: modern compiler *and* modern
headers, achieving old-system compatibility via glibc *symbol versioning*
at link time rather than by literally compiling against old headers.

Confirmed end to end:
- `perf`-profiled real installed PyPI vs conda-forge packages
  (`ExtraTreesRegressor.fit`, `n_features=30`): conda-forge spends 12.6% of
  samples in `__isnanf` alone; PyPI doesn't show it in the top 15 at all.
- Disassembled both real `.so` files directly: conda-forge's
  `find_min_max` has `call *0x1791f(%rip)  # <__isnanf@GLIBC_2.2.5>`;
  PyPI's has no call at all.
- Reproduced from source: rebuilding the actual v1.9.0 tag with the exact
  matching GCC (14.3.0-19, confirmed via the real binary's own
  `.comment` section) reproduced nothing *until* `sysroot_linux-64=2.17`
  was pinned explicitly (every environment had otherwise resolved the
  latest default, 2.39) — at which point the non-inlined call and the
  larger function size reappeared byte-for-byte.
- Same `isnan()` call pattern, same functions, confirmed still present on
  current `main` (the categorical-feature/Breiman-shortcut work added
  since 1.9.0 didn't touch this code path — `find_min_max` compiles to the
  identical byte size on both).

</details>

### Everything else that was tried and ruled out

Before finding the sysroot, a long list of variables was controlled for one at a time and **did not** reproduce the real-world gap when rebuilding from source with the real conda-forge `gcc_linux-64`/`gxx_linux-64` toolchain:

<details>

- `-O2` vs `-O3` in isolation (~1.7% effect — this is the Meson bug above)
- `-march=nocona -mtune=haswell` vs no override
- GCC version: 16.2.0, 13.4.0, and the exact `14.3.0-19` patch build
  (pinning `gcc_impl_linux-64`/`gxx_impl_linux-64`/`binutils_impl_linux-64`
  precisely, since `gcc_impl_linux-64` has its own build-number sequence
  independent of the `gcc_linux-64` wrapper)
- Cython version (real binary uses 3.2.5; early rebuilds had picked up
  3.3.0 by default — controlled for, no effect)
- Exact v1.9.0 source tag vs current `main`
- Editable install vs literal `python -m build -w` wheel build (matching
  `build.sh` exactly)
- `-fno-merge-constants` (the extra flag conda-forge adds under
  `CONDA_BUILD=1`)
- joblib version, core-count detection, BLAS threading config — all
  identical between real PyPI and conda-forge installs

</details>

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'll open the PR very soon.

issues.title: BUG: LogisticRegression (and other GLMs) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data
issues.body:
> [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact scikit-learn's linear models split into two families with very different handling of un-centered features: - `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `Lasso`, `ElasticNet` go through `_preprocess_data`, which centers `X` and `y` (explicitly for dense data, algebraically for sparse) before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. Centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed `coef`, shifting `X` by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the L1/L2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal `coef` is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. Ridge/Lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - `LogisticRegression`, `PoissonRegressor`, `GammaRegressor`, `TweedieRegressor` (the `LinearModelLoss` + `NewtonSolver`/lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do **not** do this. The intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw `X`. There is no `_preprocess_data`-equivalent step. The same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. Concretely: - `newton-cholesky` builds its Hessian from the raw `[X, 1]` design. Eliminating the intercept column during Cholesky factorization implicitly computes `X.T @ X - n * mean(X) * mean(X).T` which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. The scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - `lbfgs` doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with **no warning at all**. User-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong `coef_`/`intercept_` for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. I stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in #34793 (Ridge's cholesky centering trick). ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Sweep used to generate the plot below:
```python import warnings import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import ( LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Ridge, TweedieRegressor, PoissonRegressor, ElasticNet, ) def relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio( linear_estimator, dtype="float32", random_seed=0, max_ratio=1e5 ): rng = np.random.RandomState(random_seed) n_samples, n_features = 5000, 5 X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features)) true_coef = rng.normal(size=n_features) proba = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ true_coef))) y = (rng.uniform(size=n_samples) < proba).astype(int) X, y = X.astype(dtype), y.astype(dtype) linear_estimator.fit(X, y) ref = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() assert np.linalg.norm(ref) > 0.1 # we want coefs that aren't too small ratios = np.logspace(0, np.log10(max_ratio), num=30) errors, has_warnings = [], [] for offset in ratios: with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: linear_estimator.fit((X + offset).astype(dtype), y) shifted = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() errors.append(np.linalg.norm(shifted - ref) / np.linalg.norm(ref)) has_warnings.append(bool(caught)) return ratios, np.array(errors), np.array(has_warnings) models = [ Ridge(solver="cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), Ridge(solver="lbfgs", positive=True, alpha=1 / 5000), ElasticNet(alpha=1 / 5000), LinearRegression(), # GLMs: LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs"), LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky"), TweedieRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), TweedieRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), ] dtypes = ["float32", "float64"] n_cols = 2 n_rows = -(-len(models) // n_cols) # ceil division fig, axes = plt.subplots( n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(5 * n_cols, 3 * n_rows), sharex=True, sharey=True ) axes = axes.ravel() for ax, model in zip(axes, models): results = [relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio(model, dtype=dtype) for dtype in dtypes] for (ratios, errors, has_warnings), dtype in zip(results, dtypes): line, = ax.plot(ratios, errors, label=dtype) ax.scatter( ratios[has_warnings], errors[has_warnings], marker="x", s=10, color=line.get_color(), ) ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02) ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_title(str(model), fontsize=9) ax.tick_params(axis="x", which="both", labelbottom=True) ax.set_xlabel("mean/variance ratio") for ax in axes[len(models):]: ax.axis("off") for ax in axes[::n_cols]: ax.set_ylabel("relative error") axes[0].legend() fig.tight_layout() ```
### Expected Results Fitting on `X + offset` should not change `coef_` (more than floating point noise) or at the very least should not change `coef_` without a warning. ### Actual Results The grid below (generated by the reproducer snippet) sweeps the feature mean/variance ratio (`X + ratio`, unit-variance `X`) from 1 to 1e5, one subplot per estimator, and plots the relative error of `coef_` against the ratio=0 reference, for both `float32` and `float64`, with `×` marking points where a warning was raised: - `Ridge`, `LinearRegression`, `ElasticNet` (top two rows, the `_preprocess_data` family): error stays ~0 across the entire range, in both dtypes. issues.title: ARDRegression.scores_ combines updated precisions with the previous posterior

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Luis. I’m starting to contribute to scikit-learn by working through focused issues in its Bayesian linear models. I noticed this behavior while investigating `ARDRegression` after the discussion on #35026, and wanted to report a reproducible example before proposing a change.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `compute_score=True`, `ARDRegression` computes the posterior covariance and coefficients, updates `alpha_` and `lambda_`, then calculates `scores_` using the **updated precisions** but the **previous covariance and residual sum of squares**. As a result, the last score can differ from the objective evaluated at the fitted parameters. This can mislead users who inspect `scores_` to monitor optimization or compare the final score with an evaluation at the fitted parameters. Fitted coefficients and predictions appear unaffected

This is separate from whether the objective should include normalization constants: the comparison below omits the same constants as the current implementation.

If `scores_[-1]` is intended to report the objective at the fitted parameters, its covariance, coefficients, residuals, and precisions should correspond to the same parameter state.

There is also a related question for pruning: once the active feature set is stable, the determinant uses the covariance of retained features, while the score sums `log(lambda_)` over **all** features. Should the score represent evidence for the retained-feature model, or a limiting form of the full model? Clarifying that definition would help determine the appropriate treatment of pruned features.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import ARDRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
X = rng.normal(size=(12, 4))
y = X @ np.array([1.2, -0.5, 0.0, 0.8]) + rng.normal(
    scale=0.3, size=12
)

reg = ARDRegression(
    max_iter=1,
    compute_score=True,
    fit_intercept=False,
    threshold_lambda=1e12,
    alpha_1=0.2,
    alpha_2=0.3,
    lambda_1=0.7,
    lambda_2=1.2,
).fit(X, y)

alpha, lam = reg.alpha_, reg.lambda_
A = np.diag(lam) + alpha * (X.T @ X)
mu = alpha * np.linalg.solve(A, X.T @ y)
sse = np.sum((y - X @ mu) ** 2)

score_at_fitted_parameters = (
    (reg.lambda_1 * np.log(lam) - reg.lambda_2 * lam).sum()
    + reg.alpha_1 * np.log(alpha)
    - reg.alpha_2 * alpha
    + 0.5 * (
        -np.linalg.slogdet(A)[1]
        + X.shape[0] * np.log(alpha)
        + np.log(lam).sum()
        - alpha * sse
        - np.sum(lam * mu**2)
    )
)

print(reg.scores_[-1])
print(score_at_fitted_parameters)
```

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, this prints approximately `-5.488435` and `-7.335993`. No features are pruned in this example. The calculations use the same unnormalized objective, so omitted constants do not explain the difference.

### Expected Results

The final `scores_` entry should equal the objective evaluated at the fitted `alpha_` and `lambda_`. For this reproducer, that value is approximately `-7.335993011208482`. Each score should use the posterior and precisions from the same iteration.

### Actual Results

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, the reproducer prints:

```text
-5.48843505092349
-7.335993011208482
```

The first value is `reg.scores_[-1]`; the second is the objective recomputed at the fitted parameters. They differ by approximately `1.847558`.

### Versions

```shell

executable: <local path>\Python314\python.exe

Python dependencies:

Built with OpenMP: True

    num_threads: 16
```

Yes. I would be interested in working on a PR after the issue is triaged. The likely cause of the no-pruning discrepancy is that the score uses updated precisions with a posterior covariance and residual sum of squares computed before the update. I would make the score use a consistent parameter state and add a regression test for the reproducer. I would also confirm the intended objective after feature pruning with maintainers before changing that case.

issues.title: BUG: trees `fit(..., check_input=False)` silently ignores missing values

labels.name: Needs Decision
labels.description: Requires decision

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`DecisionTree*.fit(X, y, check_input=False)` silently ignores missing values: with `check_input=False`, `_fit` skips `_compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask`, so `missing_values_in_feature_mask` stays `None` and the splitter treats NaNs as regular values. No error, no warning, just a wrong tree (NaN thresholds, spurious depth).

And there's no way around it from the public API: the mask can only be passed to the private `_fit`. That's what forests do (they compute the mask once and pass it to each tree via `tree._fit(..., check_input=False, missing_values_in_feature_mask=...)`).

Within scikit-learn, the only caller of the public `fit(..., check_input=False)` is `BaseGradientBoosting` (`_gb.py`), which is safe only because it rejects NaNs upfront. So this mostly affects third-party code using `check_input=False` (which the docstring discourages: "Don't use this parameter unless you know what you're doing").

More broadly, a single boolean isn't enough to express "this input was already validated" for trees anymore: callers also need to provide the missing-values mask (and, with categorical support, the encoding info). Possible ways forward:

1. **Compute the mask even when `check_input=False`** on the public `fit` (when none is provided). It's one pass over `X`, cheap compared to building a tree, and makes the result correct.
2. **Document** that missing values aren't supported with `check_input=False`. Cheap, but leaves a silent trap.
3. **Deprecate `check_input` in the public `fit`** of trees, and switch gradient boosting to `_fit` (like forests). With 1. applied during the deprecation cycle.

I'd go with 3.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [np.nan], [np.nan], [2.0], [3.0]], dtype=np.float32)
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0])

for check_input in (True, False):
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X, y, check_input=check_input)
    print(f"{check_input=}: depth={tree.get_depth()}, thresholds={tree.tree_.threshold}")
```

### Expected Results

Same tree for both (or at least an error for `check_input=False`):

```
check_input=True: depth=1, thresholds=[inf -2. -2.]
```

### Actual Results

issues.body:
When https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32073 is merged, `n_jobs` will have no effect in `LogisticRegression` so should be deprecated.

It's also a good time to consider enabling multi-threading to compute the logistic regression path here https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/21e0df780772e9567b09249a05a42dfde6de465d/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py#L1373-L1388

So far it was disabled because parallelism was happening at a higher level using joblib. Now we should benchmark the impact of enabling multi-threading to see if it's positive for all the solvers and a wide range of problems.
Like for other estimators using OpenMP-based multi-threading, the number of thread should not be controlled by `n_jobs` but instead use all available core (`n_threads = _openmp_effective_n_threads()`).

issues.title: Add support for NumPy `StringDType`
issues.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`numpy.dtypes.StringDType` (and other new-style DType classes) crash `xp.isdtype()` across many sklearn utilities.

`numpy`'s (and array-api-compat's) `isdtype()` raises `TypeError` instead of returning `False` for numpy's new-style DType classes. sklearn calls `xp.isdtype(...)` in many places expecting `False` for unrecognized dtypes, not a crash.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
np.isdtype(np.dtypes.StringDType(), "numeric")
# TypeError: dtype argument must be a NumPy dtype, but it is a <class 'numpy.dtypes.StringDType'>.
```

```python
from sklearn.utils.multiclass import type_of_target
type_of_target(np.array(["a", "b", "a"], dtype=np.dtypes.StringDType()))
# TypeError: dtype argument must be a NumPy dtype, but it is a <class 'numpy.dtypes.StringDType'>.
```

Confirmed crash sites (14), all via `xp.isdtype()` except `unique_labels`:

| Function | File |
|---|---|
| `check_array` (any `dtype=`, incl. `None`) | `utils/validation.py` |
| `type_of_target` | `utils/multiclass.py` |
| `_is_integral_float` | `utils/multiclass.py` |
| `_assert_all_finite` | `utils/validation.py` |
| `_randomized_range_finder` | `utils/extmath.py` |
| `_safe_accumulator_op` | `utils/extmath.py` |
| `_find_matching_floating_dtype` | `utils/_array_api.py` |
| `_average` | `utils/_array_api.py` |
| `label_binarize` | `preprocessing/_label.py` |
| `LabelBinarizer.inverse_transform` | `preprocessing/_label.py` |
| `RidgeClassifier.fit` | `linear_model/_ridge.py` |
| `_encode` | `utils/_encode.py` |
| `_check_unknown` (→ `OrdinalEncoder.fit_transform`) | `utils/_encode.py` |
| `unique_labels` (`np.dtype(y.dtype, metadata=...)`) | `utils/_unique.py` |

Not affected: `is_multilabel`, `LabelEncoder.fit`, `_array_indexing`, `_determine_key_type`.

Related: #34383 (motivation — proposes `StringDType` internally in encoders), #9777 (same failure pattern, closed).

### Expected Results

Unrecognized dtypes should be treated like any other unsupported dtype (e.g. return `False`/`"unknown"`), not raise.

### Actual Results

`TypeError` at every site listed above (`unique_labels` raises via a different call, same root cause).

### Versions

```shell
Python 3.11.15
scikit-learn 1.8.0 and 1.9.1 (both confirmed broken)
numpy 2.4.4
pandas 3.0.2
polars 1.44.0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

One internal helper, e.g. `_safe_isdtype()`, wrapping `xp.isdtype()` to catch `TypeError` and return `False`, used at all sites above instead of patching each individually.

issues.title: Possible performance improvements for kd-tree or ball-tree with multi-threading at fit time
issues.body:
As reported here: https://skops.readthedocs.io/en/latest/auto_examples/plot_intelex.html

For small `n_features`, `KNeighborsClassifier` uses either BallTree of KD-tree algorithms. At this time, scikit-learn builds this tree sequentially.

We could recursively build the branches in parallel using a `ThreadPoolExecutor` instance and call submit for each children of a given node. Note that each node splitting operation (starting from the root) is one Cython function call that releases the GIL, so using thread-based parallelism should be efficient.

The second speed-up reported in plot_intelex.html above (at inference time) is mostly linked to the fact that scikit-learn `KNeighborsClassifier` does not enable parallel neighbors queries with the default value of `n_jobs` when using the kd-tree or ball-tree algorithms.

From a user's point of view, this is not ideal either: when using the brute-force algorithm, we rely on OpenMP and automatically use as many threads as CPUs available.

In forest algorithms, the preferred parallelization backend is `threading`. However, it looks that it is not anymore the most appropriate backend. As discussed [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/discussions/20651#discussioncomment-1124431), it might be that the GIL is not explicitly released in some part of the code locking the execution of the thread.

We need to investigate more to solve this issue.

issues.title: CPU oversaturation/oversubscription due to third-party libraries when running containers on Linux

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Background

This is the result of a discussion with @ogrisel and @jeremiedbb, fleshed out and with some additional ideas. I make my suggestion at the end, but will require feedback before I do any of the work.

### The problem

When using a container on Linux (Docker, Kubernetes, anything using cgroups), you can set a CPU quota, something like "this process gets 2 cores worth of compute."

Unfortunately, not all third-party C libraries know this. At minimum OpenBLAS does not seem to know about this limit (). So if you have 64 core machine, and run a Kubernetes pod with 8 cores, and OpenBLAS will think it has 64 cores, and it will be much much slower. Similarly libgomp and libomp. MKL builds on OpenMP so maybe no point in filing there until libgomp/libomp are fixed.

* https://github.com/OpenMathLib/OpenBLAS/issues/6059
* https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=127651
* https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/225493

This is a performance problem for scikit-lean users.

### Demonstration

My CPU has 12 cores. I set up a cgroup with equivalent of 2 cores, but OpenBLAS still reports 12 cores:

```
$ systemd-run --user --scope --property CPUQuota="200%" -- python -c "import threadpoolctl; import numpy; print(threadpoolctl.ThreadpoolController().lib_controllers[0].get_num_threads())"
12
```

### Potential fixes

I am going to be fixing one case as a side-effect of https://github.com/joblib/joblib/issues/1846: when using `joblib.Parallel`, the number of cores will be constrained using `threadpoolctl`, including in sequential cases. However, this is a strange fix where if you don't use `joblib`, you still have the same performance problem.

So what else can be done until OpenBLAS any other relevant libraries fix this issue?

#### Option 1: joblib or scikit-learn set the limit correctly, on import

Instead of doing this in `Parallel` in the sequential case, do it on import of `joblib` or maybe `sklearn`: `threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))`.  (Technically this won't fix the above example because of https://github.com/joblib/loky/issues/634 but it will work in Docker or Kubernetes, and everywhere once that issue is fixed).

Pros:

* Fixes the limit for all use cases.

Cons:

* Importing a library changing global configuration. This is not very nice.

#### Option 2: sklearn sets the limit whenever calling into OpenMP or OpenBLAS

Pros:

* If you do `with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))` it undoes the limits when done, so it's not a _permanent_ global config change, it's just DTRT.

Cons:

* This adds performance overhead of all these calls.
* Lots of code changes.

#### Option 3: Documentation of the problem and how to solve it

Pros:

* No impacts on global behavior.

Cons:

* Most people won't notice the documentation.
* If the situation improves or changes, most people won't re-read the updated docs.

#### Option 4: Warn on import

If `os.process_cpu_count() > joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1)` then that means cgroups is restricting CPU count further, so warn the user and tell them what to do. In practice should probably also docs to explain in more detail.

Pros:

* More likely to be noticed than docs.

Cons:

* Users will still have to do work.

### My suggestion

After further thought, I think setting the limit on import (option 1) is actually reasonable. The hope is that this is a stop-gap and can eventually be removed once the relevant libraries DTRT, and in practice for the vast majority of people this is the right thing to do.

If that's not acceptable, docs + warning is what I would suggest doing.

I can proceed with either, once there is some consensus.

issues.title: permutation_importance computes non-zero importance for features the model never uses when max_samples < 1

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm an undergraduate economics student at UC Davis. I use scikit-learn for data analysis and use permutation importance to understand which features matter. This is my first issue filed against scikit-learn.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**What:** When `max_samples` is set below 1, features that the model never uses still get non-zero permutation importances. By definition, shuffling a column the model does not look at cannot change the predictions, so its importance should be exactly 0. With `max_samples=1.0` the importance is indeed 0; the problem only appears when a subsample is used.

**My example:** The model only uses feature 0; features 1 and 2 are pure noise that the model never reads. With `max_samples=0.5`, both features 1 and 2 get an importance of −0.0104. The 5 repetitions (`n_repeats=5`) return exactly the same value, so the standard deviation is 0. The bias changes in magnitude and sign with the subsample size: −0.026 at 0.2 and +0.006 at 0.1. This shows it is sampling noise, not a real feature contribution.

**Cause** (I read `sklearn/inspection/_permutation_importance.py`): The baseline score is computed on all rows, while the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. The difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing to do with the feature. The docstring says a fresh sample is drawn for each repetition; in practice the subsample is drawn once per feature before the repetitions, and all features share the same random seed — so repeating does not average the bias away (std = 0), and every irrelevant feature gets the same bias.

**Impact on users:** `max_samples` exists to save time on large datasets. With this bug, irrelevant features get spuriously positive or negative importances, which can make them look useful or harmful, and can also corrupt feature ranking.

**AI usage disclosure:** I used an AI assistant to help identify this problem and write the reproduction script. The description above is my own, and the reproduction was run on my own computer.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(sklearn.__version__)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n = 200
X = rng.randn(n, 3)
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + rng.randn(n)          # only feature 0 matters
X[:, 1:] = rng.randn(n, 2)                # features 1, 2: pure noise
model = LinearRegression().fit(X[:, :1], y)  # model uses ONLY feature 0 ...
class OnlyFirst:                              # ... wrapped so it accepts 3 columns
    def fit(self, X, y): return self
    def predict(self, X): return model.predict(X[:, :1])
    def score(self, X, y): return r2_score(y, self.predict(X))
est = OnlyFirst()

r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=0.5, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=0.5):", r.importances_mean)
print("importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):")
print(r.importances[1:])

# Independent expectation: permuting a column the model never reads cannot change
# predictions, so the permuted score equals the score on the SAME rows -> importance 0.
r_full = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=1.0, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=1.0):", r_full.importances_mean)
print("baseline (all rows) r2:", r2_score(y, est.predict(X)))
for ms in (0.2, 0.1):
    r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=ms, random_state=0)
    print(f"max_samples={ms}: importances_mean =", r.importances_mean, " importances_std =", r.importances_std)
```

### Expected Results

For every repetition, the importances of features 1 and 2 should be exactly 0 — identical to the result with `max_samples=1.0`.

### Actual Results

```
1.9.1
importances_mean (max_samples=0.5): [ 1.7655429  -0.01042625 -0.01042625]
importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):
[[-0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625]
 [-0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625]]
importances_mean (max_samples=1.0): [1.79471992 0.         0.        ]
baseline (all rows) r2: 0.9095261981105188
max_samples=0.2: importances_mean = [ 1.76648851 -0.02631336 -0.02631336]  importances_std = [0.30605997 0.         0.        ]
max_samples=0.1: importances_mean = [1.66914758 0.00620688 0.00620688]  importances_std = [0.73546823 0.         0.        ]
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.14.7 (main, Aug  5 2026, 10:29:49) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)]
executable: /Users/luca/Projects/oss-contrib/.venv-skl/bin/python
   machine: macOS-26.6.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.1
          pip: 26.2.1
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.5.3
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
     narwhals: 2.26.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'd be willing to fix this. Idea: draw a fresh subsample for every repetition, and compute both the baseline and the shuffled scores on the same subsampled rows before subtracting. Add a regression test asserting that features the model does not use have exactly 0 importance when `max_samples < 1`.

issues.title: Native categorical splitting enhancements in DecisionTree, ExtraTree, RandomForest and ExtraTrees

labels.name: Hard
labels.description: Hard level of difficulty

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

From: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354#issue-3973551384, we want to enable:

1. [ ] [Optimization] Add a bitset cache (i.e. a uint64_t memory view) that allows us to compute the category split as we traverse the tree for inference speedup
2. [ ] [Feature] Support in tree-based ensemble models (RF + ExtraTrees). This could be done after for random splitter support, so we do all the classes at once: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34832/
4. [x] [Refactor] Consolidate the goes_left operation to work at inference time too: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33972
5. [x] [Refactor] Understand the bitset operations and merge these with the HistGradientBoosting bitset operations https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354)
6. [x] [Feature] Implement categorical splitting for RandomSplitter for ExtraTrees. Pretty easy now that we have an arbitrary sized bitset, which we can expand to hold many categories in the case of a randomized tree: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33972
8. [ ] [Feature] Add support for categorical in exporting 
9. [x] [Feature] Add internal ordinal encoding support for any kind of "categorical input" (see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354#discussion_r3199995969)
10. [ ] [Refactor] Address refactoring to use ColumnTransformer in tree, similar to HGBT: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354#discussion_r3521665892
11. [ ] Add warm_start capability with categorical_features (see: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34832#discussion_r4003388745_)

Below the line for priority:
1. [ ] [Feature] Brute-force search; expands categorical support to multi-class and multi-output problems
2. [ ] [Feature] Add support for sparse categorical splitting with best and random splitter

### Describe your proposed solution

These work streams may not all be relevant, or mergable, but we can explore.

issues.title: In encoders, switch to faster string representation than `object` dtype
issues.body:
Right now, `sklearn.preprocessing._encoders.BaseEncoder._check_X` has on its list of tasks "convert list of strings to object dtype". This is bad from a performance perspective, since:

1. You now have a pile of Python objects, and end up doing a lot of Python operations.
2. Interactions that involve missing data are extra expensive; I'm going to submit a separate issue/PR to speed one code path, but there may be others.

There are two superior alternatives available, that would allow bypassing Python altogether:

* NumPy's StringDType, with [custom support for missing data](https://numpy.org/devdocs/user/basics.strings.html#missing-data-support) - you can avoid using annoying nans, for example. Would require NumPy 2.0, but possibly a newer version if sklearn hits any bugs that were fixed in subsequent versions.
* Arrow string arrays, with Arrow's built-in support for missing data. Would require PyArrow, or some other Arrow library.

As an alternative to just switching completely internally, it would also be possible to add support for one, the other, or both in addition to object-based dtypes. Then users who have sufficiently new NumPy or PyArrow already installed would benefit from faster runtime, while still preserving backwards compatibility.

pulls.title: PERF New parallelism API with lower overhead
pulls.body: `joblib.Parallel` has significant performance overhead. `sklearn.utils.parallel.Parallel` has even more. That means parallelism becomes pointless in some cases, because the overhead of using these APIs drowns out the benefits of parallelism. This PR introduces a new parallelism API with lower overhead, and switches the IsolationForest prediction algorithm to use it instead of `Parallel()` as a demonstration of the benefits. ### Background https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/28622 introduced parallelism for IsolationForest prediction. However, it did _not_ enable parallelism by default, because for smaller samples the overhead made the parallel version slower. ### Speed-up of `IsolationForest` enabled by this PR With this PR, the speed of predicting large number of samples is essentially the same (so I omitted this from the plots below because it obscures the improvements on small numbers of samples). However, because of lower overhead: * Parallelism is now almost always faster than parallelism. Even in the worst case, previously it was much faster in the 100 samples case, now it's only slightly worse given how much faster all of this is for 100 samples. * For smaller number of samples, the lower overhead speeds up results. Here's a plot of before and after using this API, generated with `bench_plot_isolation_forest_predict.py` (with the 50,000 sample case disabled; for that value there's no benefit in the new API): ### Question for reviewers Since parallelism is now useful in almost all cases, and less harmful when it's not, it is worth turning it on by default? ### AI: None ### Future work * New APIs can now be parallelized, e.g. on free-threading; see #34747 which I will update and resubmit if/when this PR gets merged. * Swapping out `ThreadPoolExecutor` for a faster thread pool (e.g. https://github.com/Quansight/spinningjenny/) can reduce parallelism overhead even more. See numbers in #34747 for an example.

pulls.title: DEP deprecate LogisticRegression parameters C, introduce new regularization parameter alpha
pulls.body:
### Reference Issues/PRs
Closes #28711.
Related to #11865.

**Update June 2026** (scikit-learn sprint)
**Update August 2026** with https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32042#issuecomment-5216986708

### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR
- for class `LogisticRegression`
  - deprecates parameter `C` in 1.10
    - will raise warning in 1.12
    - will remove `C` in 1.14
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alpha`
  - ~~sets default `alpha="1/n_samples"` such that it is the same as `C=1`~~
  - sets default `alpha=1` which  is  equivalent to `C=1`
- for class `LogisticRegressionCV`
  - deprecates the parameter `Cs` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alphas`
  - deprecates attributes `C_` and `Cs_` in 1.10, removal in 1.14 
  - introduces new attributes `alpha_` and `alphas_`

<details>

**NOTE**: This "details" contains the outdate/old content.

**Update March 2026** after merge of #32659.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR
- for class `LogisticRegression`
  - deprecates parameter `C` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alpha`
  - ~~deprecates the parameter `penalty`~~
  - ~~changes the default of `l1_ratio` from `None` to `0`~~
- for class `LogisticRegressionCV`
  - deprecates the parameter `Cs` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alphas`
  - deprecates attributes `C_` and `Cs_`
  - introduces new attributes `alpha_` and `alphas_`
  - ~~deprecates parameter `penalty`~~
  - ~~changes the default of `l1_ratios` from `None` to `(0,)`~~
- for class `StackingClassifier`
  - Additional informative warning for default `final_estimator=None` which uses `LogisticRegression()`
 
</details>

**Update August 2026** see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32042#issuecomment-5216986708:
The scaling of the penalty is chosen with minimum change:
- `alpha = 1/C`
- `LogisticRegression` is then aligned with `Ridge`
- `LogisticRegression` penalty `alpha` is then different from
  - `SGDClassifier(alpha=.., loss="log_loss")` (despite #21891)
  - `ElasticNet(alpha=.., l1_ratio=..)`
  - `Lasso(alpha=)`
  - `PoissonRegressor(alpha=)` 

For historians, the parameter `scale_C` which devided `C` by `n_samples` was once deprecated in #821.

<details>

**Note:** This is outdated content as of August 2026

**Note:** Together with #32659, the way to specify penalties is then 100% aligned with 
- `SGDClassifier(alpha=.., loss="log_loss")` (this is even the identical model!), see  #21891
- `ElasticNet(alpha=.., l1_ratio=..)`
- `Lasso(alpha=)`
- `PoissonRegressor(alpha=)`
- other GLMs

All use `1/(2n) * sum(deviance loss) + alpha/2 * ||w||_2`. See #15657 for further reasons of this choice.

</details>

<details>

**NOTE:** This is outdated content.

#### Open questions
1. Default `alpha`
   While the future default is currently `alpha=1`, a much smaller value might be better in practice, e.g. alpha=1e-4. Tiny regularization is also the main effect of `C=1` as it scales the penalty by 1/n_samples.

   For optimal prediction $p=P(Y|X)$, the expected log loss is the Shannon entropy (up to a factor) $E[log loss] = H(p) = -p \log(p) - (1-p)\log(1-p)$. The maximum is achieved at p=0.5 with H=0.69, some more values: H(1e-3) = 0.007, H(1e-6) = 1.5e-5. This shows, that `alpha=1` is a pretty strong penalty (for features of scale 1 or smaller).

2. Depending on the default of `alpha`, a good default for `StackingClassifier(final_estimator=..)` is basically no or tiny regularization.

</details>

### Any other comments?
This will be a highly controversial issue, therefore a lot of fun ahead 🎉 

<details>

**Outdated content**
**The main reason for this change is that the current API is objectively bad design.** ~~Currently, I need to specify 3 parameters (`penalty`, `C`, `l1_ratio`) for just 2 effective parameters (the L1 and L2 penalization). On top, it warns a lot when mixing those, e.g. `penalty="l2"` and `l1_ratio=0`, but why on earth...~~

</details>

#### More arguments for `alpha` instead of `C`
1. API consistency: LogisticRegression is the only linear model using an anti-penalty `C`, all the others use penalty `alpha`, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28711#issuecomment-2030156413.
4. Literature:
  - The invention of using a Ridge penalty with logistic regression, https://www.jstor.org/stable/2347628 (Cessie et al 1992), uses a penalty (like `alpha`) and not an anti-penalty (like `C`). The papers for Lasso & Elastic-Net in combination with logreg do the same (use penalty like `alpha`).
  - I have a hard time (=I did not succeed) to find any (famous) ML book like ESL using the anti-penalty.
5. Other reference packages: The most famous R package glmnet (and others) uses a penalty (like `alpha`, they call it `lambda`, but that does not work in Python) and not an anti-penalty (like `C`).
6. Point of view of optimization: the penalty (like `alpha`) version can be seen as regularization to prevent singular behaviour (analogous to Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm), see Nocedal.
7. Original decision and discussion: I cannot find any discussion about the original introduction of `C` vs. `alpha` in LogisticRegression in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commit/2993becc3dde6c15b11e0f79a05dc8bc022fd9cb. My guess is that liblinear's parameter names were just inherited.
8. Practicality: One never needs `C=0` (`alpha=np.inf`), but `C=np.inf` (`alpha=0`) is used very often. Zero is a much better defined value than infinity.
9. `C` interferes with class weights. Higher class weights means less regularization.
10. The main reason for `C` (and IFAIC its origin) is the analogy with support vector machines. SVM were once very powerful, but have become less and less important in practice. My prediction: this trend will continue.

#### Study of possible default values for the penalty
See https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32042#issuecomment-4366344257 and the linked notebook https://github.com/lorentzenchr/notebooks/blob/master/logistic_regression_optimal_penalty.ipynb.
